summary: TechCrunch's running guide to Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud and money laundering trial over the collapse of FTX and Alameda Research, published as the defense phase begins and SBF is set to testify. It recaps the first three weeks: opening statements, testimony from Gary Wang, Caroline Ellison, Can Sun and others, and explains how to follow the case. Former prosecutor Josh Naftalis calls SBF taking the stand a "Hail Mary."
one_line: TechCrunch's rolling recap of the SBF trial, covering weeks one to three of testimony as the defense phase and Bankman-Fried's own testimony begin.
key_facts: Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO and co-founder of FTX, faces seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering.
The defense phase began after prosecutors finished their case, and SBF was confirmed to take the stand along with a handful of other witnesses.
Former federal prosecutor Josh Naftalis called SBF testifying a "Hail Mary," noting that once cross-examination starts, "he doesn't get to say, 'I'm done.'"
FTX went from the third-largest crypto exchange, valued at a peak of $32 billion, to bankruptcy.
Jury selection began October 3; no devices are allowed in the courtroom, and reports are put together physically in the courtroom or overflow rooms.
Caroline Ellison, Alameda Research's former CEO, testified she took $14 billion from customers to repay lenders, using them as a line of credit under SBF's instruction.
Ellison testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts, though there are no bribery charges in the case.
Former FTX general counsel Can Sun testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for using billions in consumer funds days before FTX filed for bankruptcy.
Robert Boroujerdi of Third Point testified the hedge fund made a $60 million investment in FTX and would not have invested had it known of the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX.

Professor Peter Easton of the University of Notre Dame, who helped prosecute Enron and WorldCom, testified that user deposits were used to buy real estate, make investments and fund political causes and charities.
Prosecutor Thane Rehn said in opening statements, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people."
Defense attorney Mark Cohen said SBF and colleagues "were building the plane as they were flying it."
FTX co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified that Alameda pulled funding directly from FTX customers; he gave testimony following a guilty plea in December 2022.
Paradigm, whose co-founder Matt Huang testified, invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit over promoting FTX.
